findings.title: Unrelated change: cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
findings.body: The diff changes `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)` in `Run`. This is not mentioned in the PR description and has nothing to do with the MySQL deadlock fix. It makes every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs, query history, annotations) run ten times as often, with a 9-minute timeout per run. This should be reverted or split into its own PR with a stated rationale.

findings.title: Routine progress messages logged at Error level on every batch
findings.body: The new fetch-then-delete loops log informational messages with `r.log.Error(...)`: 'Annotations to clean by time', 'cleaned annotations by time', 'Annotations to clean by count', 'cleaned annotations by count', 'Tags to clean', and 'cleaned tags'. These run for every batch, including batches that delete nothing, and they fire every cleanup cycle (once a minute now). This will flood error logs and trigger error alerting even on healthy systems. They should be Debug (or Info) messages. The `err` key is also always nil in the success-path log lines, which is misleading.

findings.title: Full ID lists logged on every batch, potentially up to the batch size
findings.body: Each batch logs the full `ids` slice (`"ids", ids`), and the batch size is configurable and can be as large as 32767 in the new test. Each cleanup batch therefore writes tens of thousands of IDs into the log, repeated on every batch and every cycle. Log the count only, or log IDs at Debug level.

findings.title: Fetched IDs are deleted without re-checking the condition, so the delete is not guarded
findings.body: The IDs are selected in one statement and deleted in a separate one with no transaction. Between the two, a concurrent update could change a row so it no longer matches (for example, a row's `created` changes). This is probably acceptable for cleanup, and the comment acknowledges the under-delete case, but the delete statement does not repeat the age or type condition, so a row that no longer qualifies can still be removed. Consider including the original condition in the DELETE, or document this explicitly as accepted behaviour.

findings.title: Large-batch test inserts about 40k rows on every run and is gated only by -short
findings.body: The new case inserts 40003 annotations and 80006 annotation_tag rows through the store in 500-row batches for each of the three cleanup cases. This is slow on every integration run and is the only coverage of the SQLite parameter limit path in `deleteByIDs`. The SQLite-specific inline-ID branch has no unit test that checks the generated SQL or the case where the batch size exceeds 999 on a non-SQLite database. Consider a unit test for `deleteByIDs` SQL generation.
